subject: math

objective.text: Solve word problems involving the total value of a group of bills.

explanations.title: Order the bills
explanations.text: Put the bills in order from greatest to least. Count the tens by tens. Count on by fives. Then add the ones.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 1 (S: greatest to least, skip-counted by tens, then fives, then ones)

explanations.title: Put together
explanations.text: To find the total of many bills, find the value of each kind of bill. Then add the parts. A tape diagram or number bond shows the parts and the whole.

explanations.title: Take from
explanations.text: When money is spent, add up the bills spent. Then subtract from the money you started with. The whole is what you started with.

explanations.title: More and less
explanations.text: Words like more and less can be tricky. Find one total first. Then check that the drawing shows who has more and who has less.

explanations.title: A drawing that makes sense
explanations.text: A drawing with a question mark for the unknown shows what you need to find. Some drawings are quicker than others, but a drawing must make sense.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 1 (the important thing is that a drawing makes sense)

examples.title: Alyssa's wallet
examples.text: Alyssa has 3 ten-dollar bills, 5 five-dollar bills and 12 one-dollar bills. 30 plus 25 plus 12 is 67. Alyssa has 67 dollars.

examples.title: Silas's gift
examples.text: Silas spent 2 twenty-dollar bills, 3 five-dollar bills and 4 one-dollar bills. That is 59 dollars. He started with 80 dollars. 80 minus 59 is 21. Silas saves 21 dollars.

examples.title: Deste and Kirsten
examples.text: Deste has 4 ten-dollar bills and 6 five-dollar bills. That is 70 dollars. Kirsten has 25 dollars less. 70 minus 25 is 45. Kirsten has 45 dollars.

visual_generation_rules: Diffusion cannot count reliably. Any picture where an exact number of objects matters must be built by code (SVG or widget) or drawn by an artist.
Diffusion is allowed only for: style or background art, and single icons (one ball, one pencil, one leaf, one character) that code then tiles to the exact count.
Every visual must be checked by a person: the count shown must equal the stimulus in the question and the rubric answer key.
Animations are described as frames with exact counts per frame, so they can be built or generated and then checked frame by frame.
Visual explanations are valid only when the asset exists (pipeline doc, Planner rules).
